metadata.title: Choosing a Journal That Will Say Yes
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.source: inbox/term2-week03/term2-week3-video-content.md (Week 3); narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27)
metadata.note: Project update. Thesis: journal choice isn't only topical fit; it's fees, agreements and realistic odds. Credit: the pipeline is Thejus's and Janvi's; journal research and reformatting are Janvi's; the journal decision was the professor's. Narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27). Only Professor Brown is named; the other professor is 'my professor'.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure + Thejus credited.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about choosing a journal for our paper, and reformatting the paper to fit it. This narration is an AI-generated voice; the work is mine. The paper covers the pipeline Thejus and I built for the Medhavy textbook.

props.command: Which journals can we publish our paper in for free, and what would I have to reformat?
props.segment: Choosing a Journal That Will Say Yes
output: Check which journals your agreements cover

beats.role_note: Constraint card 'free to publish: no out-of-pocket fee' (rule from Professor Brown); two tool chips: CRITIQ · research → SciFree · confirm coverage, under 'Northeastern open access agreements'.
beats.narration_text: The first rule came from Professor Brown: publication had to be free, with no article processing charge out of our pocket. So I checked which journals Northeastern's open access agreements cover, using CRITIQ for the research and Northeastern's SciFree tool to confirm coverage.
beats.visual_intent: Constraint card 'free to publish: no out-of-pocket fee' (rule from Professor Brown); two tool chips: CRITIQ · research → SciFree · confirm coverage, under 'Northeastern open access agreements'.

show.event: free to publish: no out-of-pocket fee

beats.role_note: Table of five options × columns fit / fee covered; rows reveal on each spoken name; no impact factors shown.
beats.narration_text: I compared five options, including JAMIA, the Journal of Biomedical Informatics, Education and Information Technologies, ACM conferences, and an AI-in-education journal, by fit and whether the fee was covered.
beats.visual_intent: Table of five options × columns fit / fee covered; rows reveal on each spoken name; no impact factors shown.

show.event: table header: option · fit · fee covered

beats.role_note: Three round cards left to right: 1 CS methodology → 2 bioinformatics ('CS angle not novel enough') → 3 'dedicated bioinformatics journals: not free'.
beats.narration_text: Then the framing changed three times. First, computer science methodology. Then bioinformatics, because the CS angle wasn't novel enough. But the dedicated bioinformatics journals weren't free under our agreements.
beats.visual_intent: Three round cards left to right: 1 CS methodology → 2 bioinformatics ('CS angle not novel enough') → 3 'dedicated bioinformatics journals: not free'.

beats.role_note: JBI card selected (teal) on 'standup call · my professor chose'; quote card 'We just want to get it published'; footer 'practical over aspirational'.
beats.narration_text: On a standup call, my professor chose the Journal of Biomedical Informatics. His reasoning was simple: we just want to get it published, somewhere that gives us an answer quickly. A practical choice over an aspirational one.
beats.visual_intent: JBI card selected (teal) on 'standup call · my professor chose'; quote card 'We just want to get it published'; footer 'practical over aspirational'.

show.event: quote: We just want to get it published

beats.role_note: Left: JBI section order stack; right: five abstract part chips and a word bar with a 300 limit line; counter 345 → 285.
beats.narration_text: Then I reformatted everything to the journal's guidelines: a new section order, and a structured abstract with five required parts, cut from 345 words to 285, under the 300-word limit.
beats.visual_intent: Left: JBI section order stack; right: five abstract part chips and a word bar with a 300 limit line; counter 345 → 285.

beats.role_note: Checklist with ticks: 5 highlights < 85 characters · MeSH keywords · Vancouver [1]–[22], no gaps · body ~3,900 words; '23 hours'.
beats.narration_text: I also wrote five highlights under 85 characters each, added MeSH keywords, converted every citation to numbered Vancouver style, one through twenty-two, and checked the numbering had no gaps. That week took 23 hours.
beats.visual_intent: Checklist with ticks: 5 highlights < 85 characters · MeSH keywords · Vancouver [1]–[22], no gaps · body ~3,900 words; '23 hours'.
